definition: Computational semantics is a subfield of computational linguistics.
details: Its goal is to elucidate the cognitive mechanisms supporting the generation and interpretation of meaning in humans. It usually involves the creation of computational models that simulate particular semantic phenomena, and the evaluation of those models against data from human participants. While computational semantics is a scientific field, it has many applications in real-world settings and substantially overlaps with Artificial Intelligence. Broadly speaking, the discipline can be subdivided into areas that mirror the internal organization of linguistics. For example, lexical semantics and frame semantics have active research communities within computational linguistics. Some popular methodologies are also strongly inspired by traditional linguistics. Most prominently, the area of distributional semantics, which underpins investigations into embeddings and the internals of Large Language Models, has roots in the work of Zellig Harris. Some traditional topics of interest in computational semantics are: construction of meaning representations, semantic underspecification, anaphora resolution, presupposition projection, and quantifier scope resolution. Methods employed usually draw from formal semantics or statistical semantics. Computational semantics has points of contact with the areas of lexical semantics (word-sense disambiguation and semantic role labeling), discourse semantics, knowledge representation and automated reasoning (in particular, automated theorem proving). Since 1999 there has been an ACL special interest group on computational semantics, SIGSEM.

explainer.lead: Computational semantics builds computer models of how people produce and understand meaning, then tests those models against human data. It matters because tasks such as resolving pronouns, interpreting ambiguous sentences, and reasoning about text all require more than recognizing words.

tiers.eli5: Think of a sentence as a puzzle whose pieces can fit together in more than one way. Computational semantics teaches computers possible ways to assemble the puzzle, such as figuring out who "she" refers to. Researchers then compare the computer's choices with what people understand.
tiers.practitioner: Its methods appear in meaning-representation construction, anaphora resolution, word-sense disambiguation, semantic role labeling, and reasoning over knowledge. Implementations may draw on formal semantics or statistical methods, including distributional representations and embeddings. A common pitfall is treating fluent output or a plausible representation as evidence that the model captures human interpretation without evaluating it against participant data.
tiers.paperLevel: The central problem is to construct a computational model M of semantic generation or interpretation and evaluate its predictions against human behavioral data. Methods range from formal representations of phenomena such as presupposition projection and quantifier scope to statistical and distributional semantics; the latter, which informs embeddings and investigations of large language models, has roots in Zellig Harris's work. The field's scientific aim is explanatory as well as practical, so predictive success alone does not establish that M reflects the underlying cognitive mechanism.

explainer.example: The sentence "Every student read a book" can mean that each student read some possibly different book, or that one particular book was read by every student. A formal model can represent these as ∀x(student(x) → ∃y(book(y) ∧ read(x,y))) and ∃y(book(y) ∧ ∀x(student(x) → read(x,y))), then test which readings people accept and prefer.

explainer.intuition: Meaning is not just a label attached to a sentence: it can depend on word senses, sentence structure, earlier discourse, and unresolved alternatives. Computational semantics makes those interpretations explicit enough to model and test.
howItWorks: Choose a semantic phenomenon, such as pronoun interpretation or quantifier scope.
Build a formal or statistical model that generates candidate meanings.
Represent how context and linguistic structure select or constrain those meanings.
Collect relevant judgments or other data from human participants.
Evaluate the model's predictions against the human data and revise it.
explainer.whyItMatters: It connects practical language technologies with a testable account of human interpretation. It also provides tools for handling ambiguity and connecting language to reasoning, rather than treating meaning as an unexplained by-product of text processing.
misconceptions: It is not only about dictionary meanings of individual words; it also studies discourse and sentence-level interpretation.
It is not limited to hand-written logical rules; statistical and distributional methods are also central.
A model that produces a plausible answer has not necessarily explained the human cognitive mechanism behind it.
